To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we developed a new, fast, radioactivity-free, high-throughput protocol for determining protein–RNA interactions that can be performed in living cells.

we have developed a novel method to determine RNA-binding sites of RNA-binding Proteins (RBPs), which we call FLASH (Fast LIGATION of RNA after Affinity Purification and High-throughput sequencing), which is fast (1.5 days), sensitive and specific, and which we have used to identify the RNA-binding sites of a variety of RBPs under different conditions.
we developed a fast, flexible, high-resolution method that enables the determination of RNA–protein interactions under various conditions in living cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method to determine RNA–protein interactions.
the development and application of FLASH, a new method for the high-throughput and high-resolution determination of RNA–protein interactions.
the development and application of FLASH to determine the RNA targets of RBPs in living cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the FLASH technique has the potential for a wide range of RNA–protein interaction studies in cells.
the FLASH protocol is a fast, simple, flexible and versatile method to identify RNA–Protein interactions in vivo, which can be applied in a wide range of biological systems.
FLASH is a powerful method that allows the identification of in vivo RNA–protein interactions with high sensitivity, high throughput and low cost.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a new method for identifying RNA targets of RNA binding proteins in vivo.
we have developed a method for the rapid determination of RNA–protein interactions.

we developed a fast, flexible, high-resolution and high-throughput method for determining RNA-binding proteins in cells, and that we demonstrated its utility by applying it to a number of different scenarios.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the FLASH approach is highly flexible and can be applied to any RBP and any cell type.
FLASH can be used in a wide array of experimental settings, including in primary cells, to determine protein–nucleic acid binding in living cells.
FLASH can be applied to any protein that can be immunoprecipitated and that it is highly amenable to high-throughput screening of protein targets.
